title: Social sciences at the centre of HIV stigma reduction

Expediting a UNIVERSAL first-line regimen of a dolutegravir–emtricitabine–tenofovir alafenamide fixed-dose ratio for children living with HIV older than 4 weeks: a 24-week, open-label, single-arm, phase 1–2, pharmacokinetic, safety, and antiviral activity trial
abstract: Background Paediatric antiretroviral fixed-dose combination tablets remain limited. UNIVERSAL1 evaluated pharmacokinetics, short-term safety, and antiviral activity of novel fixed-dose ratios of dolutegravir, emtricitabine, and tenofovir alafenamide in children with HIV. Methods UNIVERSAL1 was an open-label, single-arm, phase 1-2, pharmacokinetic, safety, and antiviral activity study. Children with HIV aged between 28 days and 10 years with a bodyweight between 3 kg and less than 25 kg were enrolled at three clinical research centres (one in Harare, Zimbabwe, and two in Kampala, Uganda). Children were enrolled across five WHO bodyweight bands (ten children per weight band) and received dolutegravir, emtricitabine, and tenofovir alafenamide at the following respective doses according to weight band: 5 mg, 15 mg, 1·88 mg (3 kg to 0-24h ) for dolutegravir, emtricitabine, and tenofovir, and from time 0 h to time of the last measurable concentration of the dosing interval (AUC 0-last ) for tenofovir alafenamide; maximum plasma concentration (C max ) for all four compounds; and concentration at the end of the dosing interval (C trough for dolutegravir, emtricitabine, and tenofovir and C last for tenofovir alafenamide). Primary safety outcomes were the occurrence of serious adverse events; new clinical and laboratory grade 3 and 4 adverse events; and adverse events of any grade leading to treatment interruption, discontinuation, or modification. Pharmacokinetic parameters were determined by non-compartmental analysis. The number of children with dolutegravir C trough lower than 0·32 mg/L (EC 90 ), tenofovir alafenamide AUC 0-last lower than 55 h × ng/mL (antiviral activity target), and tenofovir AUC 0-24h higher than 2586 h × ng/mL (toxicity target) is reported. The trial is completed and registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT05993767. Findings Between Jan 7 and June 5, 2025, 53 participants were enrolled (51 included in pharmacokinetic analysis, 53 included in safety analysis). Of these 53 children, 28 (53%) were female and 25 (47%) were male. Median age was 37 months (IQR 10-64), and median weight was 11·6 kg (7·9-16·8). Dolutegravir geometric mean (GM) value of AUC 0-24h was 93·1 h × mg/L (percentage coefficient of variation 41), C max was 7·2 mg/L (44), and C trough was 1·7 mg/L (55). No child had dolutegravir C trough lower than 0·32 mg/L. Emtricitabine GM of AUC 0-24h was 11·1 h × mg/L (60), C max was 1·6 mg/L (63), and C trough was 0·06 mg/L (46). Tenofovir alafenamide GM of AUC 0-last was 207·1 h × ng/mL (101), C max 125·2 ng/mL (114), C last 6·9 ng/mL (180). Three children had a tenofovir alafenamide AUC 0-last lower than 55 h × ng/mL. Tenofovir GM of AUC 0-24h was 219·0 h × ng/mL (53), C max 14·4 ng/mL (50), and C trough 6·9 ng/mL (66). None had tenofovir AUC 0-24h higher than 2586 h × ng/mL. Adverse events were reported in 31 (58%) of the 53 participants. The overall incidence of adverse events was 3·7 events per 100 person-weeks (95% CI 2·5-5·2). Three (6%) participants experienced a serious adverse event (hospitalisation for severe malaria, severe acute malnutrition, and life-threatening anaemia); all serious adverse events were deemed unrelated to study drugs. One grade 3 adverse event (elevated aspartate aminotransferase) was considered possibly related to the study drugs. The patient with severe malnutrition (grade 4) had to have a dose reduction due to a change to a lower weight band; no other participants experienced adverse events that led to study drug withdrawal, interruption, or modification. Interpretation These data support proposed dosing of the dispersible fixed-dose combination (dolutegravir [5 mg]-emtricitabine [15 mg]-tenofovir alafenamide [1·88 mg]) for children weighing between 3 kg and less than 20 kg and extension of the licensed film-coated tablet (dolutegravir [50 mg]-emtricitabine [200 mg]-tenofovir alafenamide [25 mg]) for children weighing 20 kg or over. Funding Second European and Developing Countries Clinical Trials Partnership (EDCTP2).

title: Advancing a fixed-dose combination for children with HIV
Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease in people living with HIV: a framework for integrated screening and care
abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) has emerged as a major cause of liver-related and cardiometabolic morbidity and mortality among people living with HIV, driven by ageing, obesity, type 2 diabetes, and long-term antiretroviral therapy. Approximately 20-41% of people living with HIV have MASLD, and significant liver fibrosis affects 12-20% of all people living with HIV, suggesting a fibrosis burden that exceeds that of the general population. HIV-specific mechanisms, including chronic immune activation, altered adipose distribution, and historical exposure to older antiretroviral agents, contribute to a more severe metabolic liver phenotype. Sex, gender, and social determinants of health-including menopause, food insecurity, and material deprivation-further influence fibrosis risk and access to care. International guidelines now recommend routine fibrosis screening in at-risk people living with HIV with the use of non-invasive tools such as transient elastography and serum biomarkers. Lifestyle interventions, optimisation of metabolic comorbidities, and emerging therapies including glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists are reshaping management. Inclusion of people living with HIV in MASLD therapeutic trials remains a major, unmet research priority.

title: Turkish Government crackdown on HIV and LGBTQ+ groups
Trends in HIV-1 transmission in Switzerland: a retrospective molecular epidemiology study
abstract: Background The rapid identification of emerging transmission clusters could help reach the 2030 goal of halting transmission of HIV in Switzerland. We characterised the size, structure, and growth of recent HIV-1 transmission clusters in the Swiss HIV Cohort Study (SHCS). Methods In this retrospective molecular epidemiology analysis in Switzerland, we analysed 32 294 HIV-1 pol sequences from 16 428 SHCS participants, enrolled between Aug 14, 1984, and May 19, 2025. Sequences were aligned and clustered using a 0·01 Tamura-Nei 93 distance threshold, and networks were constructed at the participant level to identify clusters and their growth. We defined and described a set of fast-growing clusters of HIV in Switzerland. Associations between clustering, demographic and clinical characteristics, and viral suppression were assessed. Findings 7387 (45·0%) participants were part of 1131 clusters. Cluster size distribution was highly skewed: 62% contained only two individuals, whereas a few large clusters accounted for thousands of participants. The epidemic fragmented from a single dominant cluster of people who inject drugs in the 1990s into numerous smaller clusters, predominantly among gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men (MSM). Since 2016, 32·6% of the total cluster growth was concentrated in a set of 23 fast-growing clusters. These fast-growing clusters mostly comprised western European MSM with high rates of condomless sex. Cluster growth was strongly associated with viraemia among connected participants. Interpretation The Swiss HIV epidemic has evolved into fragmented, short transmission chains, with a small number of fast-growing clusters sustaining ongoing transmission. Molecular surveillance can identify such clusters, enabling tailored interventions that complement treatment as prevention. Achieving zero HIV transmission in Switzerland will require integration of molecular epidemiology into routine prevention. Funding Swiss National Science Foundation.

title: Psychedelic-assisted therapy research for people with HIV
Integrating long-acting injectable cabotegravir for HIV prevention into the Brazilian public health system (ImPrEP CAB Brasil): a hybrid type-2 implementation-effectiveness cohort study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Daily oral pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) requires sustained adherence, which remains challenging in real-world settings. Although long-acting injectable cabotegravir (CAB-LA) could improve prevention coverage, implementation evidence in Latin America is scant. We evaluated the feasibility of integrating same-day CAB-LA delivery within Sistema Único de Saúde (SUS), the Brazilian public health system. METHODS: ImPrEP CAB Brasil was a multicentre, hybrid type-2 implementation-effectiveness, open-label cohort study done at 14 PrEP public health services in six Brazilian cities. Eligible participants were cisgender men, non-binary people assigned male at birth, and transgender men and women who have sex with men, aged 18-30 years, who tested HIV negative, and were PrEP-naive. Participants could choose either CAB-LA (CAB-LA choice cohort) or oral PrEP with tenofovir disoproxil fumarate and emtricitabine (oral PrEP choice cohort), We included a comparison cohort of people initiating PrEP in SUS (oral PrEP SUS cohort). The main outcomes were HIV incidence and follow-up days covered by PrEP. For CAB-LA, we evaluated on-time injection adherence, switching, loss to follow-up, and safety. Participants were given the option to switch PrEP modalities or remain off PrEP during follow-up. Adverse events of special interest in participants using CAB-LA were assessed at every study visit. The study was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05515770) and is ongoing. FINDINGS: Participants were enrolled from Oct 17, 2023, to Sept 16, 2024, and followed up until Oct 16, 2025. 3096 participants were included in this analysis: 1201 (38·8%) in the CAB-LA choice cohort, 246 (7·9%) in the oral PrEP choice cohort, and 1649 (53·3%) in the oral PrEP SUS cohort. Most participants were cisgender men (2893 [90·9%]), Pardo or Black (1663 [53·7%]), and completed secondary education or higher (2517 [81·3%]). Median age was 26 years (IQR 23-28). HIV incidence was 0·20 per 100 person-years (95% CI 0·04-0·57) for the CAB-LA cohort (three new HIV infections), 0·87 (0·11-3·16) for the oral PrEP choice cohort (two new HIV infections), and 1·48 (0·88-2·33) for the oral PrEP SUS cohort (18 new HIV infections). 590 091 (90·8%) follow-up days were covered by PrEP in the CAB-LA cohort versus 69 491 (47·3%) in the oral PrEP choice cohort and 328 025 (35·5%) in the oral PrEP SUS cohort (p<0·0001). 107 (8·8%) of 1220 participants were lost to follow-up in the CAB-LA cohort, and were mainly people who were non-White, had lower levels of education, and had moderate or severe depressive symptoms. On-time injection adherence was high (92%). Injection-site reactions were the most frequent adverse event (4212 events in 1067 [87·5%] participants) and were generally mild to moderate. 80 serious adverse events were reported: 43 adverse events of interest (one related to CAB-LA) and 37 other events (none related to CAB-LA). INTERPRETATION: Same-day CAB-LA delivery effectively reduced HIV incidence and increased PrEP coverage, supporting the implementation of long-acting options within SUS in Brazil. FUNDING: Unitaid, WHO, and Ministry of Health of Brazil. TRANSLATIONS: For the Portuguese and Spanish translations of the abstract see Supplementary Materials section.

Long-term immunogenicity and efficacy of the quadrivalent human papillomavirus vaccine in women with HIV: a longitudinal cohort study
abstract: Background Understanding the impact of the human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine in women with HIV, who have higher rates of HPV infection and associated disease, is vital to achieving cervical cancer elimination. We aimed to assess the immunogenicity and efficacy of the quadrivalent HPV (qHPV) vaccine up to 9 years in a cohort of women with HIV. Methods This longitudinal multicentre cohort study recruited girls and women with HIV aged 9 years and older from 14 clinics providing HIV and gynaecological care across Canada. Participants were administered three doses of qHPV vaccine at 0, 2, and 6 months and followed up from July 1, 2008, to June 27, 2019. Clinical data, anti-HPV serology, liquid-based cervical cytology, and HPV DNA genotyping were conducted at baseline and every 6-12 months. Immunogenicity endpoints were anti-HPV geometric mean titres (GMTs) and seropositivity rates. We assessed the effect of time-varying HIV parameters on time to seroreversion with extended Cox regression models. GMTs for an age-restricted subset (24-45 years) were compared with a published cohort with one-sample t tests. Efficacy endpoints were the incidence of persistent qHPV, genital warts, and cervical intraepithelial neoplasia of grade two and higher (CIN2+). Findings There were 228 participants in the per-protocol population, with a median age at baseline of 38·5 years (IQR 32·0-45·4), median CD4 count of 499·5 (IQR 380·8-700·0) cells per μL, and 160 (70·2%) participants had suppressed HIV viral loads ( Interpretation These data show low rates of infection and disease in this vaccinated cohort of women with HIV. Continual HIV viral load suppression after vaccination is important to ensure continued protection. title: Virological failure and treatment interruption among people with unsuppressed viral load on antiretroviral therapy: a cross-sectional analysis of Population-based HIV Impact Assessment surveys in seven sub-Saharan African countries
abstract: Background Viral load suppression among people with HIV on antiretroviral therapy (ART) remains a priority in sub-Saharan Africa. We aimed to quantify virological failure versus interruption in treatment among people aged 15 years or older with unsuppressed viral load. Methods In this cross-sectional analysis of nationally representative Population-based HIV Impact Assessment (PHIA) household surveys conducted in Eswatini, Lesotho, Malawi, Mozambique, Tanzania, Uganda, and Zimbabwe during 2019-23, we included participants aged 15 years or older with HIV who met the harmonised PHIA analytical criterion for ART use for at least 4 months. HIV RNA viral load was measured by quantitative laboratory assay, and antiretrovirals were detected in dried blood spots by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry. We classified virological failure (viral load ≥1000 copies per mL with detectable antiretrovirals) and interruption in treatment (≥1000 copies per mL without detectable antiretrovirals) and estimated survey-weighted prevalences and adjusted prevalence ratios (aPRs) using Poisson regression. Findings We included 14 834 participants: 10 418 were female (survey-weighted 66·2%), 4416 were male (33·8%), and 6423 were aged 30-44 years (43·6%). Overall viral load suppression was 92·4% (95% CI 91·6-93·0). Virological failure (4·7% [4·2-5·2]) was more common than interruption in treatment (3·0% [2·5-3·5]). Younger adults (aged 15-29 years) had a higher prevalence of both virological failure and interruption, strongest for interruption in treatment (aPR 7·61 [4·47-12·97] vs age ≥45 years). Men had higher virological failure than women (aPR 1·62 [1·20-2·18]). Compared with dolutegravir, efavirenz-based (aPR 3·64 [2·16-6·13]) and nevirapine-based, atazanavir-based, and lopinavir-based regimens (aPR 3·64 [1·90-6·96]) were associated with virological failure. Suboptimal adherence was associated with virological failure (aPR 2·06 [1·48-2·86]) and interruption in treatment (aPR 1·78 [1·16-2·75]). Interpretation Despite high overall viral load suppression and broad ART availability, both virological failure and interruption in treatment contribute to unsuppressed viral load among people on ART. Improving suppression requires optimising ART regimens and adherence support, particularly for men, and preventing or rapidly reversing treatment interruptions, particularly among younger adults. Funding President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief through the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

title: Reimagining HIV service integration
Epidemiological trends of HIV among individuals aged 15–54 years in South Africa from 2004 to 2025: a population-based, longitudinal cohort study
abstract: BACKGROUND: South Africa has mounted the largest HIV prevention and treatment programme in history, delivering substantial gains in survival and prevention of new HIV infections; however, service disruptions and recent funding losses might jeopardise these successes. There is a scarcity of high-quality, population-based empirical evidence on key epidemic metrics needed to accurately gauge recent progress towards epidemic control in South Africa. We aimed to evaluate recent progress towards HIV epidemic control in South Africa by quantifying long-term trends in key epidemic control metrics in a large population-based cohort in rural KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa. METHODS: In this population-based, longitudinal cohort study, we used prospectively collected HIV testing, sociodemographic, behavioural, and population viral load data from the Africa Health Research Institute (AHRI) health and demographic surveillance system in rural KwaZulu-Natal from 2003 to 2025. Population-based HIV surveys (encompassing individual health interview and HIV testing) take place annually in all consenting resident individuals aged 15 years or older. We used Poisson regression models to quantify trends in directly observed HIV incidence in repeat testers (aged 15-54 years) who had initially tested negative for HIV and subsequently received at least one valid HIV test result. We further analysed 11 rounds of population viral load testing conducted between 2011 and 2025. We used generalised estimating equations to quantify population viral suppression metrics and calculated trends in the incidence-to-prevalence ratio, a key metric for evaluating progress towards epidemic control. FINDINGS: Between June 24, 2003, and May 22, 2025, across the population cohort, 59 806 (65·4%) of 91 367 contacted individuals aged 15-54 years consented to participate at least once in population-based HIV testing. Of those tested, 33 754 (56·4%) were female and 26 052 (43·6%) were male, with a median age of 26·7 years (IQR 19·3-39·1) at testing date. Among 42 662 participants who initially tested HIV negative and were recontacted, 29 702 (69·6%) underwent repeat HIV testing and were included in the incidence analysis. In this group, over 182 112 person-years of observation, we observed 4852 HIV seroconversions. From 2013 to 2018, overall annual HIV incidence rates declined by 52·2% in males and 36·9% in females. We found no evidence of a continued downward trend in HIV incidence between 2019 and 2025 among either females or males. After a period of substantial decline (from 2011 to 2018), population detectable viraemia increased significantly from 2019 to 2025 by 9·6 percentage points (95% CI 5·4-13·8), remaining an estimated 30·7 percentage points (95% CI 27·2-34·3) below the UNAIDS 95-95-95 population viral suppression target. The incidence-to-prevalence ratio decreased substantially across consecutive survey rounds, from 0·132 (95% CI 0·114-0·152) in 2006 to its lowest recorded value of 0·034 (95% CI 0·028-0·042) in 2022, representing an overall 74·2% decline. After 2022, the ratio stagnated above the epidemic control benchmark of 0·03. INTERPRETATION: These epidemic metrics show that progress towards HIV epidemic control is faltering in KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa. The tools to reverse this trajectory are available; the challenge now is to ensure their sustained and effective implementation through coordinated action across research, policy, government, civil society, and international funding partners. We can, and we should, change course now if we want to achieve an AIDS-free generation in South Africa and the world. FUNDING: National Institute of Mental Health and Wellcome Trust.

Pharmacokinetics and safety of dolutegravir in term neonates exposed to HIV-1 (IMPAACT 2023): a phase 1, open-label, multicentre study
abstract: Background Safe and effective antiretroviral options are needed for neonates exposed to HIV-1, but data supporting dolutegravir use from birth are scarce. The aim of this study was to evaluate dolutegravir pharmacokinetics, safety, and tolerability in term neonates, and to identify an appropriate dosing regimen. Methods IMPAACT 2023 was a phase 1, open-label, multicentre study conducted at 15 IMPAACT sites in South Africa, Thailand, and the USA from Oct 5, 2022, to May 22, 2025. Full-term neonates weighing at least 2 kg born to women living with HIV-1 were enrolled between birth and 5 days of life. In cohort 1, infants received two single dolutegravir doses using liquid suspension or 5 mg dispersible tablets. In cohort 2, infants received dolutegravir 5 mg every 48 h until day 14 of life, then every 24 h up to week 4–6 depending on duration of local standard-of-care antiretroviral prophylaxis. In both cohorts, participants were stratified by antepartum maternal dolutegravir exposure. Intensive pharmacokinetic sampling was done around each of the two single doses in cohort 1 and at 7 days post initial dose and at week 4 of life in cohort 2. Safety and tolerability were assessed up to week 16. Primary pharmacokinetic outcomes were the last observed concentration of dolutegravir after each dose and area under the observed single-dose concentration–time curve in cohort 1, and concentration of dolutegravir at the end of the dosing interval (C trough ) and area under the concentration–time curve over one dosing interval (AUC 0–τ ) in cohort 2. Pharmacokinetic parameters were estimated by non-compartmental analysis in infants who received the dolutegravir dose under evaluation and had evaluable pharmacokinetic data from intensive sampling. Primary safety outcomes were study drug-related safety failure and safety failure from initial dosing up to 2 weeks after permanent study drug discontinuation. Safety outcomes were assessed in all infants who received at least one dose of dolutegravir and were summarised descriptively. The study is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT05406583, and is complete. Findings Of 73 screened mother–infant pairs, 48 were enrolled between Oct 5, 2022, and Jan 21, 2025. All 48 infants started the study drug and were safety-evaluable; 41 were pharmacokinetic-evaluable. In cohort 1, concentration–time profiles showed prolonged elimination and wide interindividual variability, with substantial overlap between neonates with and without antepartum maternal dolutegravir exposure. In cohort 2, geometric mean C trough and AUC 0–τ at the day 7 post initial dose visit were within target ranges. At week 4 of life, geometric mean AUC 0–τ remained within target range, whereas C trough exceeded the target range but remained acceptable. No infants in either cohort had a study drug-related safety failure during the primary safety window. Safety failure occurred in zero of 18 infants in cohort 1 and four of 30 infants in cohort 2. Two of 48 infants had grade 1–2 adverse events that were considered related to dolutegravir. Interpretation These findings support dolutegravir as an option from birth for presumptive therapy or early treatment in term infants weighing at least 2 kg. The present and future of HIV and viral hepatitis co-infection
abstract: HIV and hepatitis virus co-infection remains a major global health challenge, driven by shared transmission routes, populations with overlapping modes of acquisition, and potentially compounded disease progression. Co-infections of HIV and hepatitis B virus (HBV) and hepatitis C virus (HCV) remain prevalent, particularly among people who live in endemic areas, key populations, people who inject drugs, men who have sex with men, and migrants from endemic regions. Antiretroviral therapy is shifting towards regimens without HBV activity, increasing the risk for HBV infection or reactivation in some individuals. Although direct-acting antivirals have reduced active HCV infection considerably in many high-income settings, residual disease burden, reinfections, and inequitable access to treatment persist. Hepatitis delta virus continues to represent a severe but underdiagnosed co-infection among individuals with HIV-HBV co-infection, with insufficient global surveillance data. Acute hepatitis A and E increasingly affect people with HIV, presenting both as outbreak-related and sporadic cases, particularly in the context of suboptimal vaccination coverage. Contemporary management emphasises systematic screening, vaccination, integrated antiviral strategies, and public health interventions to reduce liver-related morbidity and mortality in people with HIV.
